title: Diogenes and the king
hookLine: Alexander offers him anything, and the Cynic asks him to stand out of his sunlight
last: IMAGO VITAE — THE IMAGE OF A LIFE.

lines: ONE MAN STAYS IN THE SUN.
cards: Corinth, Greece. Alexander, the young king of Macedon, not yet the conqueror he's about to become, comes to town, and everyone important rushes to congratulate him. One man doesn't come.

So Alexander goes to find him, lying on the ground in the sun: an old man with a stick, a cloak and almost nothing else. The young king with an army stands over the man who owns nothing, and makes him an offer.

teach.b: He was Diogenes of Sinope, the Cynic: one of the dog-like philosophers from Zeno's story, who owned nothing and said what they thought. Crates, the door-opener, is said to have learned from him.
Our source is a different Diogenes, Diogenes Laërtius, a biographer writing centuries later. Same name, no relation.
Alexander says: ask me for anything you want. Diogenes squints up and says: stand out of my light. That's it.
Offered the world, he wanted the sun back. He lived like that on purpose.
The stories say he slept in a big clay storage jar, walked around in broad daylight with a lamp, looking for a human being, and, asked where he was from, answered: I'm a citizen of the world.
He wasn't always pleasant; the stories are full of rudeness and stunts. But there was a serious point underneath.
One way to read this one: much of what people chase is a kind of shade, blocking a simple good already shining on them. And a strange ending.
Plutarch says that as Alexander walked away, his officers laughing at the old man, the king said: if I weren't Alexander, I would be Diogenes.
Maybe the king saw the one thing an empire couldn't give the Cynic, because he already had it: the light.

how: The Cynics practiced radical simplicity, living with almost no possessions; some people today borrow a gentler version, cutting back on what they own and chase to make room for simple goods.

games.q: you're Diogenes, lying in the sun. Alexander the Great stands over you and says: ask me for anything you want. what do you ask?
o: that he stand out of your light.
games.why: "stand out of my light." the king offered him the world, and what he wanted was the sun back.

practice: If there's sunlight near you, sit or stand in it; if not, a lamp or the memory of sun on your face will do. Close your eyes and feel the warmth: nothing is being offered, and nothing is needed.
When a want or a worry steps in front of it, notice the shade, and let it move aside.

wordCard.voice: Diogenes. A Cynic philosopher who, offered anything by Alexander the Great, asked only to stand out of his sunlight.

orig.note: Greek, kosmopolitēs: citizen of the world. Diogenes's answer when asked where he came from, and the root of English cosmopolitan.

carryVoice: Your line: stand out of my light. Some good things are already shining. Day thirty-four, done.
